title: How To Be A Classroom Management Rock Star https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/12/11/how-to-be-a-classroom-management-rock-star/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using a rock-star metaphor, Linsin argues that great classroom management is driven by mindset as much as technique. He outlines four qualities: having a clear, vivid vision of the ideal classroom that acts as a guide; an unshakeable belief in one's own ability to get there despite setbacks; taking full personal responsibility for classroom behavior rather than blaming outside circumstances like a rough neighborhood or difficult home lives; and being appropriately "selfish" by prioritizing one's own happiness and standards rather than accepting misbehavior as an unavoidable part of the job. The piece closes with a motivational challenge, urging teachers not to settle for a semi-satisfied career when a genuinely excellent classroom is within reach through intentional mindset shifts.
points: A clear, vivid vision of the ideal classroom functions as a guide that pulls a teacher toward that outcome.
Self-belief, especially during difficult stretches, is presented as essential to sustained classroom management success.
Taking full personal responsibility for classroom behavior - rather than blaming outside circumstances - is empowering rather than burdensome.
Prioritizing one's own happiness and standards, rather than accepting misbehavior as inevitable, is framed as a legitimate and necessary form of self-interest.
quotes: To create the classroom you really want, you need a clear vision of what it looks like. Otherwise, you’ll be a rudderless ship, bounced around by the tides of circumstance and never getting where you want to go.
The clearer your vision, and the more vivid it appears in the mind, the sooner it will come true.
Getting through tough times to become a classroom management rock star takes an unshakeable belief in yourself.

As soon as you shutter away the justifications, excuses, and 101 reasons why your students can’t behave, and take responsibility for the behavior that takes place on your watch, you’ll finally—blissfully—be empowered to create the class you really want.
When you make your happiness a priority, when you decide to accept nothing less than awesomeness for yourself and your classroom, then that’s exactly what you’ll get.
Don’t be like that coulda-shoulda-woulda rock star, playing the local clubs, semi-satisfied, never rising to meet his potential.
Why not go after what you really want? Why not create a classroom you can’t wait to get to every morning?
